gloss_en: 'Hello' — polite (-하세요 form). The all-purpose Korean greeting.
'shall I help you?' — 도와 (help) + 드릴 (humble give) + ㄹ까요 (shall I/we...?).
Native counter prefix meaning 'one'. Pairs with counters like 잔 (cup), 명 (person), 개 (general thing).
'please give (me)' — the workhorse polite request form. 주 (give) + 세요 (honorific polite).
Topic marker: 'as for the size...'. Frames the size as the topic the speaker will comment on.
'how' — interrogative adverb. Common in service questions.
'as / with / in (the form of)'. Tags the chosen variant — here, the Tall size.
Topic marker: 'as for the payment...'.
Polite future intent: 하 (do) + 시 (honorific) + 겠 (will/intend) + 어요 (polite).
'I'll do (it)' — speaker's own committed intent. -ㄹ게요 marks a promise or decision.
Humble 'I'll give'. Service speakers use 드리다 (humble give) instead of plain 주다.
'wait' (verb 기다리 + 어). Often followed by 주세요 to make a polite request.
Formal 'thank you'. -합니다 is the most formal ending — used in service, business, news.
Destination marker: 'to this address'.
'please go (for me)' — 가 (go) + 주 (give/favor) + 세요 (polite).
근처 (nearby) + -네요 (mild discovery). 'Ah, it's nearby!' — speaker just realized.
'that's right'. Confirming response. From 맞다 (to be correct).
'how much / how long' — interrogative adverb for quantity or duration.
'about / approximately'. Place after a quantity to soften it.
'we've arrived' — literally 'all came'. Set phrase used by taxi/bus drivers.
Formal copula 'it is'. Service form of -이에요 / -예요.
Polite-marking particle attached to a noun makes it a polite phrase: '카드요' = 'here's the card'.
'may you become / have'. Used in set phrases: 좋은 하루 되세요 (have a good day).
'do you need?' — 필요하 (need) + 세요 (honorific polite question).
'one' — native Korean number. Stands alone or before counters.
Topic marker: 'as for the bag...'.
원 (won, currency) + -이에요 (casual copula 'is').
'it's OK / I'm fine / no thanks'. Multi-purpose phrase; tone clarifies meaning.
'all together / in total'. Combines 다 (all) + 해서 (doing-and-so).
Same pattern as above. Casual 'is X won'.
'by card' — 카드 (card) + 로 (means/instrument particle).
'I'll do (it)' — committed personal intent.
'this side / this person here'. Standard frame for introducing someone.
Topic marker: 'as for this person...'.
'from' — marks origin / source.
Formal first-meeting phrase. Literally 'I shall meet for the first time'. Use with elders, in-laws, business contacts.
'I am called ~'. The standard formal self-introduction template: [name] + (이)라고 합니다.
'Pleased to meet you' (formal). 반가워요 is the slightly less formal version.
'from where' — 어디 (where) + 서 (contracted 에서, action site / origin).
Honorific past polite of 오다 ('to come'): 오 + 시 (honorific) + 었 (past) + 어요 (polite).
'from' — marks origin / source.
Contraction of 에 + 는. Marks the location AND topicalizes it: 'as for in Korea...'.
'how much / how long'. Asks about quantity or duration.
Honorific past polite of 있다 / 계시다 ('to be / stay'). Used because the subject is the listener — respect.
'It became / it's been'. From 되다. Used for elapsed time, age, completion.
Formal goodwill closing. Literally 'I humbly ask for [your] favor well'. Standard phrase when starting a relationship.
Subject marker — 'the bibimbap (specifically) is famous'.
'Try ~ once' frame: 한번 + verb + -아/어 봐. Friendly suggestion.
'Then / in that case'. Bridges the friend's suggestion to John's decision.
Casual committed intent: 'I'll eat (it)'. The polite version is 먹을게요.
Universal Korean welcome to a guest. Heard in shops, restaurants, hotels.
Polite future-intent question: 주문 (order) + 하 (do) + 시 (honorific) + 겠 (will) + 어요 (polite).
'Two (general items)'. 두 is the native counter prefix; 개 is the generic counter.
Casual 'and / with'. Polite equivalent: 와/과 or 하고.
'Spicy thing/food'. 매운 (spicy, attributive) + 거 (informal 것).
Polite honorific 'are you OK with ~?'. The honorific 시 inserts before -어요.
'A little'. Softens a statement — a beloved Korean conversational tool.
Contraction of 거 + 는 (topic marker on the informal 것).
Topic marker: 'as for drinks...'.
'How'. Goes with 하다 to ask how someone wants something done.
'(If it's) ~ then it's fine'. Useful for politely declining upsells: 그것만 있으면 돼요 ('only that is enough').
Formal 'thank you' — also used to end a transactional exchange.
'Excuse me / sorry but ~'. The standard opener when stopping a stranger.
Destination marker — 'to Gangnam Station'.
Honorific 시 + condition 면 + 돼요 ('is fine'). Together: 'you can take ~'. Universal pattern for instructions.
'From here'. 여기 (here) + 서 (contracted 에서, action site).
'Have to transfer'. -아/어야 돼요 expresses obligation.
Marks the location where the action (transfer) happens.
'How long / how much'. Asks duration or quantity.
'About (with a number)'. Native Korean approximation word.
'Approximately'. Attaches to a number/time. Can co-occur with 한.
'Boss / owner' (honorific 님). Standard way to address a shopkeeper or stall vendor.
'How much is it?'. The single most useful shopping phrase in Korean.
'One bag'. Native counter 한 + 봉지 (bag).
Distributive: 'per / each'. So 한 봉지에 = 'per bag'.
'A bit / kindly'. Softens the complaint about the price.
'Please give me a discount' — literally 'shave (price) for me, please'. The classic haggling request.
'No / can't do that' (literally 'not works'). Standard polite refusal.
Honorific conditional: 'if you (would) buy'. Vendor flatters the buyer with 시.
Humble 'I'll subtract for you'. 드리다 = humble version of 주다 (give).
'Then / in that case'. Accepts the counter-offer.
'Enjoy your meal' (literally 'eat deliciously'). Universal Korean food farewell from vendors, hosts, family.
'A cold (illness)'. 감기에 걸리다 = 'to catch a cold'.
'It seems I've caught (it)'. The -ㄴ/은 거 같아요 frame softens any medical claim.
'What kind of'. Use before a noun: 어떤 책 = 'what kind of book'.
'Symptoms'. Sino-Korean (證狀) — same kanji concept Japanese speakers will recognize.
Honorific 'do you have?'. 있다 + 으세요.
'Cough'. 기침하다 = 'to cough'.
'And / with' (also used as a connector after verbs and nouns).
'Hurts / is sore'. 아프다 → 아파요 in polite form. The 으-irregular drops 으 before 아/어.
'Medicine'. Sino-Korean (藥).
Honorific conditional of 먹다 (eat): 'if you take/eat'.
'(You) will get better' — 나아지다 (to get better) + 시 (honorific) + ㄹ (future attributive).
Distributive: 'per (day)'.
'How many times'. 몇 = 'how many' (small numbers); 번 = counter for occurrences.
'After meals' — 식 (meal, 食) + 후 (after, 後). Sino-Korean compound seen on every pill bottle.
Honorific polite imperative: 'please take / eat (this)'. Softer than 먹으세요.
